cim: The Outside View: How New AI Oversight Could Ripple Into Retail
cim_eredeti: The Outside View: How New AI Oversight Could Ripple Into Retail
szoveg_eredeti:
Democratic control of Congress next year sends a clear message to AI and Big Tech: We’re coming for you.

The blue wave of congressional investigations may sweep up not only AI’s impact on fashion, but brands and retailers directly.When Democrats take over the Senate in January, they will have the largest majority in more than a decade — a margin not seen since the height of the Levin era of corporate investigations, when the late Sen. Carl Levin (D-Mich.) chaired the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. Back then, PSI focused on Wall Street, putting Goldman Sachs in the spotlight with a 10-hour hearing and more than a thousand references in the subcommittee’s 639-page bipartisan report. The entire investigation, launched in response to the 2008 financial crisis, lasted about two years — the length of a full Congress.AI and Big Tech have joined Wall Street as targets in the return to old-school oversight. Take, for example, the role of AI at Amazon, the second-largest retailer by sales and a regular sponsor of red carpet fashion. In September, Sens. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) and Rick Scott (R-Fla.) asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether Amazon and Walmart suppressed Made in USA products for customers using the companies’ AI chatbots. Today, 42 percent of consumers use AI tools when shopping for fashion, according to the recent WWD x BCG Future of Fashion report — exposing brands and retailers to consumer protection scrutiny over which products shoppers see, and how products are labeled and reviewed.In the Senate, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), poised to helm the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee next Congress, would oversee the cybersecurity side of AI — and, with the committee’s sweeping investigative authority, could touch just about every part of tech. The incoming HSGAC chair has already posted a job announcement seeking “investigators and oversight counsel” — including candidates able to “find information when the ordinary routes are closed.”Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), one of the most aggressive critics of AI and Big Tech, is expected to chair the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. And Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), likely to lead the Senate Commerce Committee, will have the power to investigate AI companies — some of which, like OpenAI, partner with American fashion designers. In October, the former tech executive released an AI governance framework built on six principles for legislative and executive-branch action, including guardrails to protect “the products of human creativity.”AI and Big Tech face scrutiny on the House side, too. Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has long advocated for more oversight and hearings of AI companies. Now he will have the power to do just that. Casar, who also serves on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee (the House counterpart to HSGAC’s oversight authority), could push for oversight and regulation of just about every part of artificial intelligence — from data centers and AI-driven layoffs to surveillance pricing.Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ), the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, has also made it clear that he wants to “rein in Big Tech’s rapidly evolving artificial intelligence,” as reported by Politico. In May, Pallone launched a surveillance pricing inquiry, sending letters to 25 major retailers, including Amazon, Walmart and Target, about their use of consumer data and AI in setting prices. Pallone’s oversight of data-driven pricing comes as scrutiny grows over algorithms’ influence on how people shop, both in physical stores and online.It’s easy to think of oversight, particularly hearings, as a C-SPAN reality show — when members of Congress grill celebrity chief executive officers and other expert witnesses. But the hearing is hardly the beginning — far from it. Letters from congressional leadership, committee staff meetings and closed-door briefings start weeks, if not months, before executives ever reach the hearing room. The 2008 financial crisis, for example, led to numerous oversight hearings, and in December 2009, the late Rep. Barney Frank (D-Mass.), then chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. Levin held his landmark Goldman Sachs hearing in April 2010, the Senate passed its version of the bill in May, and President Barack Obama signed the Dodd-Frank Act into law in July 2010.Oversight of AI and Big Tech could have far-reaching effects on fashion brands and retailers. For example, with little, if any, notice to the fashion industry at the time, a conflict minerals provision was added as a floor amendment to the Dodd-Frank Act days before the Senate vote. The provision led to a 2012 Securities and Exchange Commission rule requiring publicly traded companies to disclose the use of certain minerals sourced from the strife-ridden Democratic Republic of the Congo or adjoining countries as a way to reduce support for the region’s armed conflict.Yet 16 years later, the SEC conflict minerals rule is still in effect — a reminder that what starts as part of a congressional investigation or draft legislation can have long-term implications for fashion.In 2010, it was Wall Street and financial reform. Today, it’s AI and Big Tech — with an even more direct connection to brands and retailers.Kenya Wiley is a fashion and tech policy counsel. She previously served as counsel and senior policy advisor for the U.S. Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
